title: Describe the functions of the workplace health and safety representative

lessons.title: The legal framework for HSRs
lessons.html:
The OHS Act and health and safety representatives

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 (OHS Act) is the main law for health and safety at most workplaces, including farms. (Mines fall under separate mine health and safety law.) It gives duties to employers and employees and creates the role of the health and safety representative (HSR).

Key sections

SectionTopic
Section 8General duties of employers to their employees
Section 14General duties of employees at work
Section 17Appointment of health and safety representatives
Section 18Functions of health and safety representatives
Section 19Health and safety committees

Appointment

  • An employer with more than 20 employees at a workplace must appoint HSRs in writing.
  • HSRs are full-time employees who know the workplace and the work.
  • They are appointed after consultation with employees or their union, for a period agreed in that consultation.
  • Each HSR is designated to a specific area, such as the packhouse, the dairy or the workshop.

Rights and protection

  • The employer must give HSRs the facilities, help and training they reasonably need, and allow them to do their functions during working hours.
  • No one may victimise an employee for doing their duties under the Act.
  • An HSR does not become personally liable simply because they failed to do something they may do as an HSR. Responsibility for safety remains with the employer.

The HSR is the link between the workers and management on safety. They do not replace the supervisor's duty to manage safely; they help make sure safety works in practice.

lessons.title: What HSRs do and how committees work
lessons.html:
Functions of an HSR

Within their designated area, an HSR may:

  • review how effective health and safety measures are,
  • identify potential hazards and potential major incidents,
  • examine the causes of incidents, together with the employer,
  • investigate complaints from employees about health and safety,
  • make representations (recommendations) to the employer and the committee,
  • inspect the workplace, including articles, substances, plant and machinery, at agreed intervals,
  • take part in consultations with labour inspectors and accompany them on inspections,
  • attend health and safety committee meetings.

Addressing issues within your authority

An HSR does not have the authority to discipline workers or spend company money. When you find a problem:

  1. If someone is in immediate danger, warn them and report to the supervisor at once.
  2. Speak to the worker politely and explain the safe way, such as putting on hearing protection at the grinder.
  3. Report hazards in writing, using the farm's hazard report form.
  4. Follow up to see if the issue was fixed. If not, take it to the committee.

Health and safety committees

  • Where two or more HSRs are appointed, the employer must set up one or more committees.
  • The committee includes HSRs and members nominated by the employer.
  • It meets at least once every three months, keeps minutes, and makes recommendations to the employer.
  • It discusses incidents, inspection reports, risk assessments and training needs.

Environmental issues

On farms, safety, health and environment overlap: chemical spills, waste, dust and water pollution. HSRs can raise these at committee meetings too.

Key points

  • Sections 17 to 19 of the OHS Act cover HSRs and committees.
  • Employers with more than 20 employees must appoint HSRs.
  • HSRs inspect, identify hazards, investigate complaints and make recommendations.
  • Committees meet at least every three months and keep minutes.
  • HSRs act within their authority: report, advise and follow up.
